newsitem.title: UK: Healthy stocks, rising supply spell weak oil.
newsitem.headline: Healthy stocks, rising supply spell weak oil.

text.p: The West's energy watchdog painted on Tuesday a bearish picture for oil markets, saying industry stocks had returned to good health, OPEC production was surging and alternative supplies were ample.

Slack winter demand and rising output from the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and elsewhere left stocks barely lower in the critical first three months of the year, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its latest oil market report.
Industry stocks in OECD nations were drawn down by a mere 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) in the first quarter compared with 1.5 million bpd in the same period last year, the Paris-based agency said.

"The impact of relatively mild weather on demand and strong growth in non-OPEC supply, albeit less than expected, is thought to have resulted in an abnormally small stockdraw in the first quarter 1997," the Paris-based agency said.
World benchmark Brent crude futures have slumped this year from just below $25 in early January to $17.65 last Friday, the lowest in nearly 10 months.

Brent steadied on Tuesday, trading up 20 cents at $17.96 a barrel by midday in London. While any further short-term losses are expected to be modest, traders and analysts say buyers still have the upper hand given the prospect of even higher output in the second quarter of the year.
"Weather-related demand has disappeared and the realisation that OPEC is still overproducing is coming home to roost," said Stephen O'Sullivan, associate director at MC-BBL Securities.
"On balance, there is more scope for the downside than the upside. OPEC will continue to overproduce... and non-OPEC supply will continue to rise," he said.

For the first time in five years, second quarter non-OPEC supply should exceed first quarter levels, thanks to new start-ups, repairs and upgrades to North Sea fields and accelerating Latin American production which should more than compensate for maintenance shutdowns, the IEA said.

Traders said the prospect of a bigger than normal rise in stocks this spring, due to rampant OPEC overproduction, rising Iraqi exports and higher non-OPEC volumes, would keep the oil market under pressure.
"Will it go lower? Probably a bit more but it may struggle in the West," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of the oil trading division at Bankers Trust International in London.

In the report, the IEA maintained its world demand forecast for 1997 at 73.7 million bpd, up 1.8 million bpd on 1996, but cut its estimate of the demand for OPEC oil by 100,000 bpd to 25.3 million bpd for the year.
OPEC continues to flout its self-imposed ceiling of 25.03 million bpd, producing 27.09 million bpd in March, according to the IEA.

"It seems to me that OPEC (members) are sticking to the extra production they enjoyed due to very firm prices last year despite the fact that the market has become one of surplus rather than shortage," the head of crude trading for a major North Sea producer said on Monday.
